title: Preparing a Project for Release
subtopics: Final code review and release checklist
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose and terminology of Preparing a Project for Release.
Apply or interpret one Express.js 5 pattern related to production environment configuration.
Identify a meaningful edge case and choose a repeatable local test for it.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will learn preparing a project for release and connect the named syllabus points to a small Express.js example. The course baseline is Express 5.x on a supported Node.js LTS release; the page shows reference output, not execution of Node.js code.
content.why_it_matters: Preparing a Project for Release matters because it helps keep the request/response contract explicit and the application maintainable as inputs, users and dependencies become less predictable. A releasable application, not just a demo.

content_blocks.title: Concept map: Preparing a Project for Release
content_blocks.alt_text: A conceptual three-stage flow for Preparing a Project for Release: context or input, the Express.js concept, and verification of expected behavior with an edge case.
content_blocks.caption: Use this visual to connect production environment configuration to preparing a project for release; the final step is to verify both normal and boundary behavior.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Preparing a Project for Release is part of practical application development and capstone preparation. Plan end-to-end features with acceptance criteria, integrate data and identity components behind clear contracts, review security, test the public API, and release with operational checks and documentation. For this topic, make the observable behavior explicit, then check what happens when an input is missing, malformed, unauthorized, or a dependency fails (choose the relevant cases for this lesson).

items.title: Production environment configuration
items.text: Validate required configuration at startup, keep credentials outside source control, expose a limited health check, and verify logs, deployment smoke tests and recovery steps before release.

items.title: Deployment and smoke tests
items.text: Make behavior reproducible with assertions for a normal case, invalid input, boundary values and errors. Mock external side effects in unit tests and keep separate integration checks for real boundaries.

items.title: Monitoring and logging
items.text: Validate required configuration at startup, keep credentials outside source control, expose a limited health check, and verify logs, deployment smoke tests and recovery steps before release.

items.title: Backup and recovery considerations
items.text: Connect this syllabus point to Preparing a Project for Release: state the expected behavior, identify a realistic edge case, and choose a test or observation that proves the behavior instead of relying on assumptions.

items.title: Final code review and release checklist
items.text: Define acceptance criteria before coding, integrate one vertical slice at a time, and verify the result with a repeatable test and a clear rollback/cleanup plan.

content_blocks.title: Read the example carefully
content_blocks.text: A useful way to study preparing a project for release is to start from the first syllabus point — production environment configuration — and follow it through a small request or application example. Keep Express's built-in behavior separate from optional packages and your own application policy.

content_blocks.title: Worked example (reference only)
content_blocks.code:
app.get('/health', (_req, res) => res.status(200).json({ status: 'ok' }));
// Release gate: automated tests, route contract checks, dependency review and deployment smoke test.
content_blocks.expected_output: The example illustrates the pattern; exact output depends on the supplied request and environment.
content_blocks.notes: This is a focused teaching fragment for Preparing a Project for Release. Add the error, validation, and resource-lifecycle handling needed for a complete application.

content_blocks.title: Safety / production rule
content_blocks.text: Module rule — Plan end-to-end features with acceptance criteria, integrate data and identity components behind clear contracts, review security, test the public API, and release with operational checks and documentation.

content.task: Try it yourself: adapt the worked example to demonstrate preparing a project for release. Write down the exact request or command, expected status/body, one boundary case, and how you would reset the local lab. CodeLeaf does not execute Express code in this lesson page; run Node.js server examples locally.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example has a clear local run or inspection path and the required dependencies are named.
A normal request and a malformed/edge/failure request have documented expected outcomes.
No credentials, production data, or claim of successful runtime execution is included.
hints: Hint 1: identify which part of preparing a project for release is supplied by Express and which part belongs to your own application or another package.
Hint 2: check the official Express 5 guide/API reference and isolate the smallest example that proves one behavior.
Hint 3: verify a success case, a boundary case and the expected status/response; restart from a clean state before repeating.
content.solution_notes: Suggested approach: Plan end-to-end features with acceptance criteria, integrate data and identity components behind clear contracts, review security, test the public API, and release with operational checks and documentation. The sample is a focused reference fragment. Review all dependency, schema, proxy and runtime assumptions before using it in an application.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying an example without checking its assumptions
common_mistakes.why: A fragment may omit route setup, middleware order, external packages, database schema or production configuration.
common_mistakes.fix: State the runtime/dependency assumptions, run the focused example locally, and test a success path plus one failure path.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating all request values as trusted
common_mistakes.why: Parameters, query values, body properties, files and upstream responses can be missing or malicious.
common_mistakes.fix: Validate schema, type and bounds at the boundary; keep authorization and database constraints as separate checks.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming the demo output means the server executed
common_mistakes.why: The course page shows reference output for Node.js/Express code; it is not an isolated Node runtime.
common_mistakes.fix: Run the example locally with the documented Node.js version and record actual command/output and test results.

summary: Explain the central idea behind preparing a project for release.
Connect the relevant subtopics to the request/response or application boundary.
Verify one normal outcome and one edge/error case with repeatable evidence.
run_instructions: Open a terminal in the lesson lab directory.
Install dependencies for the sample if required; use a supported Node.js LTS release.
Run the documented file with node, send the stated request with curl or an API client, and compare the actual status/body with the reference.
reset_steps: Stop the local process with Ctrl+C.
Clear only temporary/synthetic records or files created by the lab.
Restart the server before repeating the example.
troubleshooting: If node reports a module-syntax error, check package.json module type or use the matching CommonJS syntax.
If a package cannot be resolved, install the named dependency in the local lab and verify the lockfile.
If output differs, verify middleware order, the request path/method, environment variables and the expected runtime version.
